HomeEssentials Inc. - Q3 2023 Earnings Call Transcript

Operator:
Good morning, everyone, and welcome to the HomeEssentials Inc. Q3 2023 Earnings Conference Call. All participants will be in listen-only mode. After today's presentation, there will be an opportunity to ask questions. [Operator Instructions] Please also note, today's event is being recorded.

I would now like to turn the conference over to Sarah Johnson, Head of Investor Relations. Please go ahead.

Sarah Johnson, Head of Investor Relations:
Thank you, Operator. Good morning, and thank you for joining us today to discuss HomeEssentials Inc.'s results for the Q3. Joining me on today’s call are Mike Thompson, Chief Executive Officer; and Lisa Chen, Chief Financial Officer.

Before we begin, I would like to remind you that this call contains forward-looking statements, which are subject to risks and uncertainties. Please refer to our SEC filings for a complete discussion of these risks.

With that, I’ll turn the call over to Mike.

Mike Thompson, Chief Executive Officer:
Thank you, Sarah. Good morning, everyone. Thank you for joining us today. I’m pleased to report HomeEssentials Inc.'s performance for the Q3. We continued to execute on our strategic priorities and delivered solid results despite the challenging macroeconomic environment.

Our comparable store sales grew 3.2%—our strongest in over two years—while we expanded adjusted EBITDA margins by 110 basis points to 7.8%. We opened new small-format stores in high-growth markets, accelerated omnichannel fulfillment like BOPIS and curbside, optimized our digital marketing to drive traffic, and advanced key initiatives in supply chain and experiential retail. We're entering the holiday season with momentum, confident in navigating headwinds like inflation and cautious consumer spending to deliver long-term value for shareholders.

Now, I'll turn the call over to Lisa to provide more details on our financial results.

Lisa Chen, Chief Financial Officer:
Thank you, Mike. Good morning. I'll provide a more detailed review of our financial performance for the Q3.

Our total revenue for the quarter was $2.48 billion, a 4.2% increase compared to the same period last year. Gross margin was 35.2%, primarily driven by easing supply chain freight costs down 15% sequentially, favorable product mix from our private-label Everyday Home brand now at 28% of sales delivering 250 basis points of margin accretion, and inventory optimization that cut markdowns. Operating expenses were $731 million, representing 29.5% of revenue, reflecting labor efficiencies from optimized store staffing which reduced payroll per square foot by 8% year-to-date, along with productivity gains like RFID tagging in 60% of stores slashing shrinkage to 1.1% of sales. Net income was $114 million, or $0.95 per diluted share. We generated $185 million in cash flow from operations. Inventory levels are currently optimized, reduced by 12% through AI-driven demand forecasting in partnership with Blue Yonder.

We are maintaining a strong balance sheet and are well positioned to invest in our growth initiatives.

Thank you, Mike, and good morning, everyone. As we wrap up a solid third quarter where we delivered comparable store sales growth of 3.2%—our strongest in over two years—and expanded adjusted EBITDA margins by 110 basis points to 7.8%, let me turn to our outlook for the balance of fiscal 2023 and into 2024. We're entering the critical holiday season with momentum, but we're tempering expectations given the macroeconomic headwinds, including persistent inflation above the Fed's 2% target and consumer confidence readings hovering around 100 on The Conference Board's index, signaling cautious spending.

For the fourth quarter, we expect total net sales in the range of $2.45 billion to $2.55 billion, representing flat to 4% growth year-over-year. This incorporates comparable store sales growth of 1% to 3%, driven by our core home essentials categories like kitchenware and bedding, which saw +5.2% comps in Q3. We're baking in some softness from big-ticket discretionary items such as furniture and outdoor living, where comps dipped -1.8% last quarter amid higher interest rates curbing big purchases—similar to what we've seen across peers like RH and Wayfair.

Gross margins should land at 35.0% to 35.5%, up 20-50 basis points from last year, thanks to easing supply chain freight costs—down 15% sequentially—and favorable product mix from our private-label Everyday Home brand, which now accounts for 28% of sales and delivered 250 basis points of margin accretion in Q3. SG&A as a percentage of sales is projected at 29.5% to 30.0%, reflecting continued labor efficiencies from our optimized store staffing model, which reduced payroll per square foot by 8% year-to-date. This should drive adjusted operating income of $140 million to $160 million, with diluted EPS of $0.85 to $0.95, excluding any non-recurring items.

Capex for the quarter will be around $120 million, focused on high-ROI initiatives like our next-gen store prototypes. We're on track to remodel 45 locations this year, incorporating omnichannel hubs with dedicated Buy Online, Pick Up In-Store (BOPIS) zones and curbside fulfillment bays—pilots in our Dallas-Fort Worth cluster have boosted BOPIS penetration to 22% of digital orders, outperforming Target's reported 18-20%.

Pulling it all together, we're raising the midpoint of our full-year outlook. Total net sales now expected at $9.8 billion to $10.0 billion, up 3% to 5% versus prior year. Comps remain guided at 2% to 4%. Adjusted diluted EPS of $3.50 to $3.70, implying 10% growth at the midpoint and about 20% EPS expansion after adjusting for last year's COVID-related stimulus tailwinds.

Gross margins: 35.2% to 35.6%, benefiting from inventory optimization—we've reduced excess stock by 12% through AI-driven demand forecasting via our partnership with Blue Yonder, cutting markdowns by 30 basis points. Operating margins expand to 5.3% to 5.7%, with SG&A leverage of 80 basis points from productivity gains, including our shift to RFID tagging in 60% of stores, which has slashed inventory shrinkage to 1.1% of sales from 1.6% two years ago.

Free cash flow guidance holds at $450 million to $500 million, supporting $200 million in share repurchases this year under our $1 billion authorization and a 15% dividend hike we announced this morning to $0.28 per share quarterly.

Looking to fiscal 2024, we're positioning HomeEssentials for accelerated growth in a normalizing retail environment. We expect total sales growth of 4% to 6%, with comps of 3% to 5%, assuming CPI moderates to 2.5-3% and unemployment stays below 4.5%. EPS growth of 12% to 15%, targeting $3.95 to $4.20, with gross margins stable at 35.5% and operating margins expanding another 50 basis points to 5.8% to 6.2%.

Regionally, performance will vary. Our Sunbelt markets—Texas, Florida, and the Carolinas, representing 42% of our 1,200-store fleet—are firing on all cylinders with +6.1% comps YTD, fueled by in-migration and home formation trends; we're committing $250 million over two years to open 25 new stores here, including experiential formats with design studios akin to Home Depot's Pro hubs. Conversely, the Northeast and Midwest (35% of sales) face headwinds from harsh winter weather and softer housing turnover—expecting flat comps there—prompting us to harvest $50 million from closing 15 underperforming urban locations, much like Bed Bath & Beyond's recent rationalization.

Strategically, we're doubling down on tech-enabled brick-and-mortar dominance. Our omnichannel sales now exceed 45% of total, with store-fulfillment digital orders up 28% YTD. Key initiatives include: enterprise-wide rollout of SymphonyAI's retail platform by mid-2024 for hyper-personalized assortments—early tests show 15% uplift in basket size via app-based "shop the aisle" features. Private label acceleration: targeting 35% of sales by 2025, with new sustainable lines like recycled polyester bedding to capture the 25% of consumers prioritizing ESG, per Nielsen data. Supply chain resilience: full deployment of micro-fulfillment centers in 10 metros, reducing delivery times to same-day for 70% of orders and cutting logistics costs by 10-12%. Loyalty evolution: enhancing HomePerks to a tiered program with AI-recommended bundles, aiming for 65% penetration (up from 52%) and 20% higher lifetime value.

Risks to the outlook include potential tariff escalations on imported hardlines (20% of COGS) or a consumer pullback if job growth slows below 150K monthly. Upside levers: strong Black Friday/Cyber Week traffic—we're projecting 5-7% comps in holiday home—plus share gains from value messaging in a trading-down environment, where we've outpaced the Home Furnishings index by 200 basis points.

In summary, we're confident in our ability to navigate volatility through disciplined execution, delivering shareholder value while transforming our stores into indispensable community destinations.

Shifting gears, I'd like to dive deeper into one of our key growth levers: digital marketing effectiveness. As a leading brick-and-mortar retailer in the home essentials space—think furniture, appliances, and decor akin to a blend of Home Depot and Wayfair's physical footprint—our 1,200+ stores across North America rely on precision digital strategies to drive foot traffic, boost same-store sales, and enhance omnichannel conversion. In Q3, digital marketing not only exceeded our internal KPIs but also demonstrated resilience amid macroeconomic headwinds like softening consumer sentiment and elevated ad platform costs.

Our overall Return on Ad Spend (ROAS) for digital channels climbed 28% year-over-year to 9.4x, up from 7.3x in Q3 2022. This marks our strongest quarterly performance since pre-pandemic levels, driven by a 15% reduction in Customer Acquisition Cost (CAC) to $18.50 per new high-value customer—defined as those with an expected Lifetime Value (CLV) exceeding $750 over 24 months. Conversion rates from digital touchpoints to in-store transactions hit 22.7%, a 4-point improvement YoY, with Buy Online, Pick Up In-Store (BOPIS) orders surging 42% to represent 18% of total digital-originating sales. For context, this outperforms industry benchmarks from peers like Target, where BOPIS penetration hovers around 12-15%, and aligns with Walmart's omnichannel push.

Breaking it down by channel, search and social remain our heavy hitters. Google Ads and Performance Max campaigns delivered a segment-leading ROAS of 12.1x, fueled by our proprietary first-party data integration via Google Cloud's Customer Data Platform (CDP). We layered in enhanced attribution modeling—shifting from last-click to data-driven multi-touch—to capture 30% more assisted conversions from upper-funnel brand awareness efforts. On Meta platforms, Instagram and Facebook Shops drove a 35% YoY increase in shoppable post engagements, converting at 8.5% to store visits via our geofencing pixels. TikTok, our fastest-growing channel, saw a 62% spend increase but delivered outsized results with a 7.2x ROAS, targeting Gen Z millennials for impulse buys like affordable lighting fixtures and textiles—mirroring SHEIN's viral playbook but anchored to our physical inventory.

Technically, we've accelerated several initiatives to future-proof against cookie deprecation and iOS privacy changes. Our AI-powered personalization engine, built on Adobe Experience Platform and our in-house HomeMatch algorithm, segments users into 47 micro-cohorts based on purchase history, geolocation, and zero-party data from our Essentials Rewards loyalty program—now boasting 28 million active members, up 19% YoY. This enabled hyper-targeted dynamic creative optimization (DCO), where ad variants featuring AR virtual room planners increased click-through rates (CTRs) by 41% and reduced CPAs by 22%. We also piloted server-side tracking with Google's Consent Mode v2, boosting measurement accuracy to 95% and reclaiming 12% of previously 'dark' traffic.

Regionally, performance varied but trended positively. In the U.S., comprising 72% of our digital budget, urban markets like the Northeast and California saw a 17% lift in foot traffic from geofencing campaigns—alerting users within 5 miles of stores for flash promotions on big-ticket items like kitchen appliances. This drove $142 million in incremental store sales, per our proprietary lift studies using mmWave footfall counters. Midwest and Southeast regions lagged slightly at 11% lift due to softer housing starts, echoing broader RE/MAX data on subdued home improvement demand. In Europe, our 250 stores faced headwinds from energy cost inflation but achieved a solid 8.1x ROAS, with the UK leading via Snapchat AR lenses for garden decor, up 29% in conversions amid a mild spring rebound. Expansion into Germany via partnerships with Otto.de yielded early wins, with cross-border retargeting converting 14% of digital traffic to BOPIS.

Strategically, these results underscore our 'Digital-to-Door' thesis: every $1 invested in digital must yield at least 3x in physical store economics to justify brick-and-mortar CapEx. We're allocating 55% of our FY24 marketing budget—$450 million total—to performance channels, prioritizing owned media like our app's push notifications (open rates at 48%, 2.3x industry avg per AppsFlyer benchmarks). Looking ahead, we expect Q4 ROAS to hold at 9.0x+, supported by holiday black-box testing on Amazon DSP for conquesting competitors like Lowe's. Risks include rising CPMs on Meta (up 18% YoY) and potential Google antitrust rulings impacting auction dynamics, but our diversified stack and 65% first-party data reliance mitigate this.

In summary, digital marketing isn't just effective—it's the flywheel accelerating our 4.2% comps growth this quarter. We're not chasing pure ecommerce like Wayfair; we're leveraging digital to supercharge our store ecosystem, where 68% of revenue still flows.

Thank you, Mike, and good afternoon, everyone. As we wrap up our Q3 results, I'd like to provide a detailed update on our key strategic initiatives, which continue to drive sustainable growth for HomeEssentials Inc. across our 1,200+ brick-and-mortar locations nationwide. These pillars—Store Portfolio Optimization, Omnichannel Acceleration, Supply Chain Resilience, and Experiential Retail Innovation—are not just buzzwords; they're delivering measurable results amid a challenging retail landscape marked by persistent inflation, softening consumer confidence, and intensifying competition from pure-play e-commerce giants like Amazon and Wayfair.

We've made significant progress on Store Portfolio Optimization, balancing density with profitability. In Q3, we opened 18 new small-format stores—averaging 15,000 square feet versus our legacy 40,000-square-foot boxes—in high-growth Sunbelt markets like Phoenix, Dallas-Fort Worth, and Atlanta. These formats emphasize quick-turnover essentials like paint, tools, and seasonal decor, yielding an average payback period of under 18 months based on early run-rate sales of $450 per square foot annually. Comps from these new units are tracking at +12% year-over-year.

On the rationalization side, we completed the divestiture of 42 underperforming stores in the Northeast and Midwest—regions hit hard by urban exodus and a 15% YoY decline in foot traffic per Placer.ai data—generating $120 million in proceeds. This trimmed our overall portfolio by 3.5%, but boosted system-wide comp store sales to +4.2% for the quarter, outpacing the NRF's reported retail comp average of +2.1%. Post-remodel, our 150 targeted locations saw a 28% uplift in traffic and +9.5% comps, driven by refreshed layouts with dedicated "smart home" zones featuring integrations like Philips Hue and Nest products. Looking ahead, we plan 25-30 net new stores in FY24, with a bias toward the Southeast, where housing starts remain robust at 1.2 million units annualized per Census Bureau figures.

Turning to Omnichannel Acceleration, our "Seamless Home" platform is firing on all cylinders. BOPIS and curbside fulfillment now account for 32% of total digital orders—up from 22% a year ago—representing 18% of overall sales, a 450-basis-point increase. This is fueled by our revamped HomeEssentials app, which integrates AR visualization tools akin to IKEA Place, allowing customers to "place" furniture in their space via LiDAR-enabled iPhones. Adoption has surged 65% QoQ, with 4.2 million active users. We've also expanded same-day delivery partnerships with DoorDash and Uber in 75 metro areas, capturing 15% market share in urban markets per our internal ShipBob benchmarking.

A key technical enabler here is our AI-powered demand forecasting engine, built on Google Cloud's Vertex AI, which has reduced out-of-stocks by 22% across 5,000 SKUs. This directly contributed to a 150-basis-point gross margin expansion to 38.2% in Q3, as we optimized assortments away from low-margin commoditized items like basic lumber toward higher-ASP categories like sustainable appliances (up 19% YoY).

Supply Chain Resilience remains a top priority post the 2022 disruptions. We've localized 60% of our sourcing to North American vendors—up from 35% in 2021—mitigating Red Sea and Panama Canal delays that have inflated ocean freight rates by 40% per Drewry Index. Our new 800,000-square-foot distribution center in Reno, Nevada, is now at 95% capacity utilization, slashing lead times to under 48 hours for West Coast stores. Inventory turns improved to 5.8x from 4.9x YoY, and we're piloting RFID tagging on 20% of softlines inventory, targeting a 10% shrinkage reduction. Regionally, this has been a game-changer in the West, where comps hit +6.8% versus flat in the Midwest, reflecting better responsiveness to regional preferences like drought-resistant landscaping in California.

Finally, Experiential Retail Innovation is differentiating us in a sea of sameness. We've rolled out "Home Maker Labs" in 200 flagship stores—interactive zones with 3D printing for custom cabinetry pulls and VR design consultations, inspired by Lowe's holistic design centers. Guest satisfaction scores via Medallia surveys jumped 18 points to 92, driving a 14% increase in average ticket to $185. Loyalty program enrollment grew 22% to 28 million members, with personalized offers via our Einstein-powered CRM yielding 3x redemption rates. Sustainability ties in here too: our "Green Home" assortment, featuring FSC-certified woods and ENERGY STAR partners like GE Appliances, now represents 12% of sales—up 40% YoY—and resonates strongest in coastal markets where 68% of consumers prioritize eco-labels per NielsenIQ.

Strategically, these initiatives position us to capture share in a $1.2 trillion U.S. home improvement market growing at 3.5% CAGR through 2027, per Freedonia Group, even as brick-and-mortar faces headwinds from e-commerce's 15% penetration. Our omnichannel blend delivers superior unit economics: brick stores contribute 82% of EBITDA despite only 65% of sales, with ROIC at 14.2% versus industry peers' 11% median per McKinsey retail benchmarks.

In summary, these efforts underpin our raised FY23 guidance: comps +3.5-4.5%, digital sales +25%, and EBITDA margin expansion of 50 basis points to 8.2%. We're executing with discipline, leveraging our store footprint as a competitive moat in an asset-light world.

Before opening the line, let me highlight the strong momentum in our omnichannel initiatives, which continue to be a cornerstone of our transformation strategy here at HomeEssentials Inc. As you know, we've been aggressively bridging our 1,200 brick-and-mortar locations with our digital ecosystem to deliver a seamless customer experience—think Buy Online Pick-Up In Store (BOPIS), curbside pickup, ship-from-store, and now our emerging same-day delivery partnerships. This isn't just about checking boxes; it's driving outsized comp sales growth, margin expansion, and customer lifetime value in a market where pure-play e-commerce like Amazon is facing logistics headwinds amid softening consumer demand.

In Q3, omnichannel sales—defined as digital orders fulfilled through our stores—accounted for 28% of our total digital sales, up from 22% a year ago and marking our 10th straight quarter of acceleration. Overall digital penetration hit a record 42% of total company sales, with omnichannel specifically contributing 12% to total revenue, a 35% year-over-year increase. This outpaced our physical store comps of +4.2% and helped lift blended comps to +7.5%. On a two-year stacked basis, omnichannel comps are running at +52%, underscoring the durability of these channels post-pandemic.

Breaking it down by fulfillment type: BOPIS remains our crown jewel, representing 65% of omnichannel orders and growing 42% YoY. We processed over 4.2 million BOPIS transactions in the quarter, with average order value (AOV) at $78—10% above pure e-comm AOV—thanks to our targeted upsell algorithms in the app that suggest complementary in-store exclusives like our private-label kitchenware bundles. Conversion rates for BOPIS shoppers in-store hover at 68%, driving an incremental 15% attach rate on high-margin add-ons such as extended warranties and assembly services.

Curbside pickup, which we rolled out to 95% of our stores last year, saw a 55% YoY surge to 2.8 million orders, fueled by working parents and urban millennials who value the contactless convenience. Fulfillment costs here have improved dramatically to just 4.2% of sales—down 120 basis points QoQ—due to optimized store labor scheduling via our AI-powered workforce management tool, integrated with Manhattan Associates' WMS (Warehouse Management System). This is giving us a 200-300 bps gross margin advantage over third-party delivery options.

On the technical front, we've invested over $150 million YTD in our omnichannel tech stack, including a full migration to Oracle Retail's real-time inventory visibility platform across all stores. This has reduced stockouts by 37% for high-velocity SKUs like apparel and seasonal home goods, with 98% item-level accuracy for BOPIS commitments within a 10-mile radius. We've also launched 'Store Mode' in our mobile app—a geofencing feature that auto-suggests BOPIS for in-market shoppers, boosting app engagement by 24% and lifting digital wallet adoption to 62% of transactions. Partnerships are key too: our pilot with DoorDash Drive for hybrid curbside/same-day in 150 high-density stores is converting at 22% of curbside volume, with early economics showing sub-8% fulfillment costs.

Regionally, performance varies but trends are consistent. In the Northeast and West Coast urban clusters—like our 200+ stores in the NYC metro and SoCal markets—omnichannel penetration exceeds 35% of sales, driven by density and foot traffic from hybrid work patterns. BOPIS here is up 48% YoY, though we're monitoring curbside softness from easing COVID anxieties. Midwest and Southeast markets, more rural-leaning, are at 25% penetration but growing faster at 41% YoY, where curbside shines amid longer drive times—think families in Charlotte or Indianapolis stocking up on groceries and durables. Internationally, our 120 Canadian stores are at 18% omnichannel mix, accelerating with Loblaws-inspired curbside tweaks, while our UK pilot with 25 Tesco-partnered locations is hitting 15% penetration ahead of plan.

Strategically, these initiatives are fortifying our moat against disruptors. Unlike Walmart's heavier reliance on dedicated DCs (which inflated their fulfillment costs to 6-7% last quarter), our store-as-micro-fulfillment-center model leverages existing CapEx, yielding 25-30% higher store labor productivity—our associates are now handling 18% more picks per hour without headcount growth. Customer loyalty metrics are stellar: omnichannel shoppers have a 2.7x higher NPS (82 vs. 64 for pure store) and 40% higher repeat rates, with 55% of them crossing into higher-margin categories like home furnishings. Amid inflation pressures and supply chain snarls—U.S. retail inventories still 15% above pre-pandemic norms per NRF data—this gives us pricing power and inventory turns of 5.8x vs. the sector's 4.2x.

Looking ahead, we're on track to hit 30% omnichannel digital mix by FYE '25, with Q4 catalysts including Black Friday BOPIS reservations (already +28% vs. last year) and a national rollout of RFID-enabled scan-and-go curbside to cut fulfillment times under 5 minutes. CapEx allocation remains disciplined at 4.5% of sales, focused on these high-ROI levers. This positions us not just to compete, but to lead in a brick-and-mortar renaissance where physical stores drive 70% of the profit pool, per McKinsey's latest retail outlook.

Now, let's open the line for questions.

Operator:
Thank you. [Operator Instructions] Our first question comes from John Smith with Goldman Sachs. Please go ahead.

John Smith (Goldman Sachs):
Good morning. Can you provide more color on the impact of persistent inflation on your sales?

Mike Thompson, Chief Executive Officer:
Good morning, John. Persistent inflation above the Fed's 2% target has indeed led to cautious spending, as reflected in consumer confidence around 100 on The Conference Board's index. That said, our core home essentials like kitchenware and bedding are holding strong with +5.2% comps in Q3, as consumers prioritize must-haves. Big-ticket items like furniture and outdoor living saw some softness at -1.8% comps due to higher interest rates curbing large purchases, similar to peers. We're countering this with value messaging and private-label growth, which has helped us outpace the Home Furnishings index by 200 basis points. We're baking that dynamic into our Q4 comp guidance of 1% to 3%.

Operator:
Our next question comes from Emily Davis with JPMorgan. Please go ahead.

Emily Davis (JPMorgan):
What are your expectations for same-store sales growth in the next quarter?

Lisa Chen, Chief Financial Officer:
Thanks, Emily. For Q4, we're guiding comparable store sales growth to 1% to 3%, with strength in core categories offsetting some caution on discretionary big-ticket items. This supports our total net sales outlook of $2.45 billion to $2.55 billion, flat to 4% year-over-year. Regionally, Sunbelt markets remain robust at above 5%, while we're more measured in the Northeast and Midwest.

Operator:
Our next question comes from David Lee with Morgan Stanley. Please go ahead.

David Lee (Morgan Stanley):
Lisa, can you expand on the capex plans and how they tie into omnichannel?

Lisa Chen, Chief Financial Officer:
Absolutely, David. Q4 capex is around $120 million, with full-year focus on high-ROI areas like remodeling 45 stores with BOPIS zones and curbside bays. Pilots show BOPIS at 22% of digital orders. In FY24, we're prioritizing micro-fulfillment and new Sunbelt stores, keeping overall capex disciplined at about 4.5% of sales to support margin expansion.

Operator:
Our next question is from Rachel Kim with Barclays. Please go ahead.

Rachel Kim (Barclays):
How are you thinking about risks like tariffs in your outlook?

Mike Thompson, Chief Executive Officer:
Good question, Rachel. Tariffs on imported hardlines, which are 20% of COGS, are a noted risk, along with any slowdown in job growth below 150K monthly. We've localized 60% of sourcing to North America to build resilience. Upside includes strong holiday traffic, where we see 5-7% comps potential from Black Friday value plays.

Operator:
Thank you. That concludes today's Q&A. I'll now turn the call back over to Mike for closing remarks.

Mike Thompson, Chief Executive Officer:
Thank you for your questions. In closing, we are pleased with our progress this quarter and remain focused on executing our long-term strategy. Thank you for your continued support.

Sarah Johnson, Head of Investor Relations:
This concludes today's call. Thank you for joining us.
